solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Bone in a truss, tight, a girl's broken

indicators.note: tight is slang for drunk, and drunken letters reel out of their order
something broken has its parts scattered, so these letters are reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a gal is a girl

explanation.surface: A girl strapped into a tight surgical truss has broken a bone.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', not a possessive. Both 'tight' (drunk) and 'broken' signal mixing the letters of A TRUSS and A GAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The astragalus is the anatomical name for the ankle bone, or talus.

clue.text: SA hoodlum cheers stretcher

parts.note: skol is a drinking toast
a stretcher is slang for an exaggeration or untruth

explanation.surface: A South African thug raises a glass while being carried off on a stretcher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretcher' looks like a medical litter, but it is old slang for a tall story.
explanation.definitionFit: Skollie is South African slang for a young street thug or gangster.

clue.text: Lizard skin half shed

indicators.note: to shed half is to drop one of the word's two equal parts

parts.note: tegument is a formal word for a natural covering or skin

explanation.surface: A lizard has shed half of its skin, as lizards do.
explanation.walkthrough: TEGUMENT has eight letters; losing the back four leaves TEGU.
explanation.definitionFit: The tegu is a large South American lizard of the teiid family.

clue.text: Early record from Queen brought up former romance

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing something up turns it so it reads from the bottom

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual abbreviation for the Queen
a gest is an old word for a tale of adventure or a romance

explanation.surface: The Queen recalls an old love affair, documented in some early record.
explanation.walkthrough: ER turned upward gives RE, followed by GEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Regest is an archaic word for a register, a written record of events.

clue.text: Like a physical signal, a mixture of rage and lust

indicators.note: a mixture blends its ingredients together, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Body language that expresses both anger and desire at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Gestural means relating to gestures, which are physical signals made with the body.

clue.text: Dancer Ida dismissed by London theatre

indicators.note: someone dismissed is sent away, so that name is removed from the other word

parts.note: the Almeida is a theatre in Islington, north London
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dancer called Ida gets sacked by a London theatre company.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking IDA off the end of ALMEIDA leaves ALME.
explanation.definitionFit: An alme (or almah) is an Egyptian dancing girl, a professional performer.

clue.text: Legal negligence ending in funeral is painful

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, the only one kept here

parts.note: the last letter of funeral
something that aches is painful

explanation.surface: A sad remark that negligence ending in a funeral is a painful matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Laches is the legal term for unreasonable delay or negligence in asserting a right.

clue.text: Muddy tootsies, dirtier than the rest

indicators.note: to muddy things is to mix them up, so the letters are stirred into new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Some muddy little feet that are filthier than anyone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muddy' reads as an adjective for the feet; it is the instruction to mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Sootiest is the superlative of sooty, covered in soot and so the grimiest of all.

clue.text: Drunk a little red (not opening barrels)

indicators.note: not tells us to leave the picked letter out of the other word

parts.note: a blush is a slight reddening of the face

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, which is the one picked out

parts.note: the first letter of barrels

explanation.surface: A drunk downs a little red wine without first broaching the barrels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not opening barrels' means without the B that opens 'barrels', so BLUSH loses its B.
explanation.definitionFit: A lush is a slang noun for a heavy drinker, a habitual drunk.

clue.text: Caring for woods etc, hear about sudden increase in sandpipers? (11, two words)

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word is wrapped around the phrase that follows

parts.note: to hear a case in court is to try it
a ree is a female ruff, a sandpiper, and a surge is a sudden increase; the question mark admits the invented phrase

explanation.surface: A wildlife report hearing about a population boom among sandpipers in the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear' is the judicial sense, to try a case; TRY splits around REE SURGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tree surgery is the pruning, repair and care of trees, as in woods and gardens.

clue.text: Foam bits're crumbling round square of discredited insulation

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the fodder is placed around the single letter
crumbling material falls to bits, so the letters break up and re-form

parts.note: taken as written, with the contracted 're
S is an abbreviation for square

explanation.surface: Old foam lagging is crumbling around a patch of insulation now known to be dangerous.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestiform means having the fibrous form of asbestos, the insulating material discredited as a health hazard.

clue.text: Identify with Corbynite strike vigorously

parts.note: to be something is to identify with it
Jeremy Corbyn led the UK Labour Party

explanation.surface: Supporters urged to identify with a Labour leader's call to go on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' sounds like industrial action, fitting Corbyn's party, but it means hit.
explanation.definitionFit: To belabour is to beat or thrash someone soundly, an old sense besides overelaborating.

clue.text: Shelled eggs in sauce, too liquid?

indicators.note: in places the kept letters inside the word for the sauce

parts.note: soy is a sauce made from fermented soya beans

indicators.note: shelling removes the outer casing, so only the inner letters survive

parts.note: eggs without its outer letters

explanation.surface: A cook frets that peeled eggs drowned in sauce are too runny.
explanation.definitionFit: Soggy means soaked through and sodden, with far too much moisture.

clue.text: Went for madame's article

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the French word for a thing or object

explanation.walkthrough: 'Madame's' says the second meaning is French; an article here is an object, not a grammatical word like 'le'.
explanation.definitionFit: The English past tense means picked, and the French noun means a thing or item.

clue.text: Lively little piece tutee played with behind library?

indicators.note: letters that are played with are toyed about and rearranged
behind puts the mixed letters after the library abbreviation

parts.note: BL is the British Library
the letters of tutee rearranged

explanation.surface: A music student performs a sprightly short piece at the back of the library.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluette is a short brilliant piece of music, a spark of a composition.

clue.text: River landing that's nearer when river's diverted

indicators.note: a diverted river is channelled away, so it no longer flows through the word

parts.note: hither, as in the hither bank, means the nearer
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A riverside landing stage has come closer since the river changed course.
explanation.walkthrough: HITHER loses its final R.
explanation.definitionFit: A hithe (or hythe) is an old word for a small haven or landing place on a river.

clue.text: Quick chat and drinks during break in card game

indicators.note: the second word is broken open and the first sits inside during the gap

parts.note: Snap is a children's card game
nips are small measures of spirits

explanation.surface: Players chat and sip drinks during an interval in a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: The card game is opened up after its first letter to take the drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Snip-snap is quick, smart repartee, a brisk exchange of retorts.

clue.text: Aussie purloins small amounts when about to arrive in Paris

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the small amounts are placed round the verb

parts.note: a sou is a small coin, hence a very small amount
venir is French for to come or arrive

explanation.surface: An Australian pockets small change on arrival in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: In Australian slang, to souvenir something is to pinch it, so the definition is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian slang uses 'souvenir' as a verb meaning to steal, so 'souvenirs' means pinches.

clue.text: Head of finance in love is unusually articulate

indicators.note: in places the head of finance inside the following words
unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters take a different order

parts.note: taken as written
a CA, chartered accountant, heads up the finances

explanation.surface: A finance director who has fallen in love is surprisingly eloquent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of finance' is not F, the first letter, but the accountant CA.
explanation.definitionFit: To vocalise is to utter or express in words, a synonym of the verb articulate.

clue.text: Geyser deposit consisting of sulphur to treat as landfill?

parts.note: S is the chemical symbol for sulphur
to inter is to bury, as landfill buries waste

explanation.surface: A geyser's sulphurous crust, to be buried as landfill waste.
explanation.walkthrough: Inter usually means bury a body; here it is burying anything in the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinter is a siliceous or calcareous crust precipitated from hot springs and geysers.

clue.text: Creature protected in India? Some sterilize bullocks

indicators.note: some means only a part, so the letters are a run inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A question about Indian cattle protection and the practice of neutering bullocks.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: cattle are sacred to Hindus.
explanation.definitionFit: The zebu is the humped domestic ox of India, held sacred and so protected.

clue.text: Coofs trapping French lady in brasseries

indicators.note: trapping means holding something caught inside

parts.note: brasseries are bars serving food
Mme is the abbreviation for Madame

explanation.surface: Louts in French bars cornering a local woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Coof is a Scots word for a dolt or lout.
explanation.definitionFit: Bammer is a Scots word for a fool or simpleton, as is coof.

clue.text: Currency piece from Italy in basic decimal unit

indicators.note: in puts the country's letter inside the number word

parts.note: ten is the base of the decimal system
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A coin from Italy minted in a basic decimal denomination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currency piece from Italy' reads as one phrase; 'from' is just the join.
explanation.definitionFit: A tein is a monetary unit of Kazakhstan, a hundredth of a tenge.

clue.text: British girl swallowing last of pot in US rave-ups

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British

indicators.note: swallowing means taking something inside

parts.note: a lass is a girl

indicators.note: last of means only the final letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the last letter of pot

explanation.surface: A British girl drinks or smokes pot at wild American parties.
explanation.walkthrough: T goes between the two S's of LASS, after B.
explanation.definitionFit: In US slang a blast is a riotously good party or time, a rave-up.

clue.text: Delivery of a kind, a scare when batting

indicators.note: batting means flapping about, as eyelids do, so the letters are shaken up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket delivery that gives the batsman a fright.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture makes 'delivery' a ball bowled; it is a birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar is informal for a Caesarean section, a surgical way of delivering a baby.

clue.text: English name for Trèves: it's familiar to mountaineers

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
Trèves is the French name for the German city of Trier

explanation.surface: A question of what the English call the city of Trèves, as known to climbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English name' looks like one phrase; English gives only E.
explanation.definitionFit: An étrier is a short rope ladder used in climbing, a piece of gear every mountaineer knows.

clue.text: Driving force that gets pitman moving about a yard and a bit

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the miner's letters go round the measure
moving letters shift out of place into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the English ell was 45 inches, a yard plus a quarter

explanation.surface: Whatever motivates a miner to shift a little over a yard of coal.
explanation.definitionFit: An impellant is something that propels or drives forward, an impelling force.

clue.text: Holiday wandering in Far East (not Arabia)

indicators.note: wandering things drift from their path, so the letters stray into a new order
not tells us to leave the country's letters out of the phrase

parts.note: taken as written
AR is an abbreviation for Arabia or Arabic

explanation.surface: A backpacker's holiday travelling through the Far East but skipping Arabia.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing A and R leaves FEAST, which is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Festa is Italian for a festival or feast day, a holiday.

clue.text: Popular circus character, hard up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: sore can mean severe or hard, as in sore trials

explanation.surface: A well-loved clown at the circus who has fallen on hard times.
explanation.walkthrough: The circus is Piccadilly Circus in London, whose famous statue is popularly called Eros.
explanation.definitionFit: The winged statue at Piccadilly Circus, popularly called Eros, is a much-loved London landmark.

clue.text: Potential energy holding fungus back, from which plant growth starts

indicators.note: holding means keeping something inside

parts.note: PE is the standard abbreviation for potential energy

indicators.note: back means the fungus is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: the morel is an edible fungus

explanation.surface: Stored energy in a fungus kept in reserve, fuelling the start of plant growth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potential energy' gives two letters that split to hold the reversed fungus.
explanation.definitionFit: The plerome is the central core of an apical meristem, the tissue from which a plant's stele develops.

clue.text: Burnsian pie, still with a bit of pastry on it

indicators.note: in a down clue, on it means placed above the other piece
a bit of means only one letter, the first, is taken

parts.note: the first letter of pastry
yet and still both mean even now

explanation.surface: A pie of the kind Burns ate, still with a scrap of pastry on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pie' is not food but the old word for magpie; Burns wrote in Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyet is a Scots word for the magpie, the 'pie' of older English.

clue.text: One beyond the wall once lives well, having climbed up

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing up means reading from the bottom upward

parts.note: to be is to live or exist
so and well are both interjections opening a remark

explanation.surface: Someone who once lived well beyond a wall they climbed over.
explanation.walkthrough: The wall is the Berlin Wall; IS SO reads upward as OSSI.
explanation.definitionFit: Ossi was colloquial German for a citizen of the former East Germany, behind the Berlin Wall.

clue.text: Bird population of a county, not trapped by children

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits on the outside of the adjective, and only what it encloses is kept

parts.note: Cornish means of Cornwall, a county in south-west England
CH is an abbreviation for child or children

explanation.surface: A county's bird life left undisturbed by local children.
explanation.walkthrough: CORNISH has C at the front and H at the back; strip them away.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornis is the avifauna, the collective birds, of a region.

clue.text: Endless danger, tyre half gone from rear, no tread

indicators.note: endless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: a risk is a danger

indicators.note: read from the rear, a fragment runs back to front
half gone means two of four letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning about a tyre worn bald at the back, with no tread left.
explanation.walkthrough: RISK loses K; TYRE loses TY, leaving RE, read backwards as ER. 'No tread' sounds like a bald tyre but means a step's other part.
explanation.definitionFit: In a staircase the riser is the vertical board between steps, as opposed to the tread you stand on.

clue.text: Damage to treads — cause for failing this? (8, two words)

definitions.text: Damage to treads — cause for failing this?

indicators.note: damaged things are knocked out of shape, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Worn tyre treads are a reason a car would fail its inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: worn treads are a cause of failing a vehicle trial, while also supplying the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A road test is a trial of a vehicle on public roads, which bald tyres would fail.

clue.text: A pie of suet protected by solid form of inoculation

indicators.note: printer's pie is type jumbled together, so the letters are muddled
protected by means enclosed within the other word

parts.note: a prism is a geometric solid
taken as written
the letters of suet jumbled

explanation.surface: A suet pie eaten as a hardy remedy against disease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pie' is printer's pie, jumbled type; A plus the jumbled SUET sits inside PRISM after its P.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasteurism is Louis Pasteur's method of preventive inoculation, especially against rabies.
